record.original_question: Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.

evidence.quote: Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a finite group. The holomorph of $N$ is the semidirect product $\mathrm{Hol}(N) = N \rtimes \mathrm{Aut}(N)$, which acts faithfully and transitively on the underlying set of $N$ via $(n,\alpha)\cdot x = n\,\alpha(x)$. A subgroup $G \le \mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is called regular if it acts regularly on $N$ (that is, transitively and with trivial point stabilizers); equivalently, $|G|=|N|$ and $G$ acts transitively.

Prove or disprove: if $N$ is a finite soluble group, then every regular subgroup of $\mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is soluble.
artifact.category_tag: Holomorphs and regular subgroups of finite groups
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. Subsequent work has provided partial results: computational verification for small orders, and structural restrictions on hypothetical counterexamples (e.g., every non-abelian composition factor of a counterexample must be PSL(2,7) of order 168, and every maximal normal subgroup of N must have index 2). Recent papers explicitly treat the question as open and study related/generalized versions (e.g., insoluble transitive subgroups with soluble point stabilizers).

status_evidence.title: On the solvability of regular subgroups in the holomorph of a finite solvable group
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates the conjecture; provides structural restrictions on possible counterexamples (composition factors must be PSL(2,7); maximal normal subgroups have index 2).
status_evidence.claim: Partial results restricting the structure of any potential counterexample; conjecture not resolved.

status_evidence.title: On Insoluble Transitive Subgroups in the Holomorph of a Finite Soluble Group
status_evidence.snippet: Studies whether the holomorph of a finite soluble group can contain an insoluble regular subgroup, and classifies irreducible solutions in a broader transitive setting.
status_evidence.claim: Treats the original regular-subgroup conjecture as open and addresses a related, broader problem.
